cards.text: The word of the LORD comes to the prophet Ezekiel. God calls him 'son of man' and tells him to take up a lament for Tyre, the city at the gateway to the sea, merchant to peoples on many coasts. God starts by quoting what Tyre has been saying about itself.

cards.question: What has Tyre been saying about itself?

answers.text: That it is perfect in beauty
That it can never be conquered
That it is older than every city

cards.text: Tyre's borders are in the heart of the seas, and its builders perfected its beauty. Me? I came out of a closing bakery's bargain bin for 25 cents.
Then God describes the builders at work. All the planking is cypress from Senir, and they take a cedar from Lebanon to make the mast.

cards.question: With planking and a mast, God is picturing Tyre as a great ___.

cards.text: Oars of oak from Bashan, a deck inlaid with IVORY, a sail of embroidered linen from Egypt. Friend, the only thing inlaid in my bakery floor is flour, and that was an accident.

cards.question: Tyre's builders went cheap and used whatever wood was lying around.
Men of Sidon and Arvad pull the oars of Tyre's ship. So who stands as its captains?

cards.text: The elders of Gebal come aboard too. Their job? Shipwrights.

cards.question: Even Tyre's ship, perfect in beauty, has leaks that need repairing.

cards.text: Perfect in beauty, and it LEAKS, which I respect, because I spent years as a worn-out stamper with blurry edges. Then all the ships of the sea pull up alongside Tyre, sailors and all.

cards.question: Why do all the ships of the sea come alongside Tyre?

cards.text: Now the picture moves to Tyre's walls, where men of Persia, Lydia and Put serve as warriors and hang their shields and helmets. Men of Arvad and Helech man the walls, men of Gammad hold the towers, and they hang their shields all around.

cards.question: All those shields and helmets hanging on Tyre's walls add to its splendor.

cards.text: Then comes a long list of Tyre's trading partners, nation after nation: silver, iron, tin and lead from Tarshish, wheat and honey from Judah and Israel, gold and spices from Sheba. Friend, I spent years under old receipts in a junk drawer, and not ONE of them was this long.
Business is BOOMING: the ships of Tarshish carry Tyre's merchandise, and Tyre is filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea. Then its oarsmen bring it out onto the high seas.

cards.question: Out on the high seas, what does God say will shatter Tyre?
God says Tyre's sailors, captains and warriors will sink into the heart of the sea along with its wealth.

cards.text: God says the countryside will shake when Tyre's sailors cry out, and all who handle the oars will abandon their ships.

cards.question: God says the sailors and all the captains of the sea will end up standing on the ___.

cards.text: God says the sailors will throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes. They'll shave their heads and wrap themselves in sackcloth too.

cards.question: What will all that dust, ash and sackcloth from the sailors show?

cards.text: God says that as they wail, the sailors will take up a lament for Tyre, just as Ezekiel was told to. It begins: 'Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?'

cards.question: In their lament, the sailors will look back and say Tyre's abundant wealth and merchandise ___ the kings of the earth.

cards.text: Then their lament turns: Tyre is shattered by the seas in the depths of the waters, and its merchandise and people have gone down with it.

cards.question: In the sailors' lament, how do the people of the coastlands react to Tyre being shattered?
The sailors' lament ends with hope that Tyre will one day rise again.

cards.text: In the lament, the coastlands' kings shudder with fear, and those who trade among the nations hiss at Tyre. Then it closes: 'you have come to a horrible end and will be no more.'
